title: Elephants and Their Families
summary: How elephants live in herds led by the oldest female, raise their calves together, use their trunks, talk with low sounds, and why they need protection.
poll: Animals that live in families have a better chance to survive than animals that live alone.

versions.title: Big Elephant Families
versions.text:
Look at the big gray beast. It is an elephant. No land animal is as big. Some live in Africa. Some live in Asia.

Elephants live in a group. The group is a herd. It has moms, aunts, and kids. The leader is the old mom. She knows where to find food. She knows where to find water. Young males leave when they grow up.

A baby is a calf. It grows in its mom for two years. At birth, it is as big as a man. It can stand in an hour. The whole herd keeps it safe.

The long nose is a trunk. It can smell. It can drink. It can grab food. It can hug, too! Some have two long teeth. They are tusks.

They eat plants all day long. They call to each other. Some calls are too low for us to hear. They feel the calls with their feet.

Some people hunt them for their tusks. Parks help keep them safe.

Elephants live in a family group. This group is a herd. It has moms, aunts, sisters, and their young. The leader is the oldest female. She is called the matriarch. She knows where to find food and water. Young males leave the herd in their teens.

A baby elephant is a calf. It grows in its mom for close to two years. At birth, it weighs about 100 kilograms! It can stand in about an hour. The whole herd helps keep it safe.

The long nose is the trunk. It can smell, drink, and grab food. It can hug, too. Most have two long teeth. These are called tusks.

They eat plants for most of the day. They call to each other. Some calls are too low for us to hear. But they can feel them with their feet.

Some people hunt elephants for their tusks. Parks and laws help keep them safe.

versions.title: Elephants and Their Families
versions.text:
No land animal is as big as an elephant. There are two main kinds. One kind lives in Africa, and the other lives in Asia. Both kinds are smart. They care a lot for their families.

Elephants live in family groups called herds. A herd has moms, grandmas, aunts, sisters, and their young. The leader is the oldest female. She is called the matriarch. She knows where to find food and water, even in dry times. Young males stay with the herd until their teens. Then they leave. They live alone or with other males.

A baby elephant is called a calf. It grows in its mom for close to two years. A new calf weighs about 100 kilograms! It can stand up in about an hour. All the moms in the herd help care for it. If danger comes, they stand in a ring around it.

The long nose is called a trunk. It has lots and lots of muscles. It can smell, breathe, drink, pick up food, and hug. Most elephants also have two long teeth called tusks.

They eat grass, leaves, bark, and fruit for most of the day. They also send deep calls to each other. Some calls are too low for us to hear. But elephants can feel them with their feet.

Sadly, some people hunt elephants for their tusks. Parks and laws now help keep them safe.

versions.title: Elephants and Their Families
versions.text:
Elephants are the biggest animals on land. There are two main kinds. African elephants live in many parts of Africa. Asian elephants live in the forests and grasslands of southern Asia. Both kinds are smart. Both care a lot for their families.

Elephants live in family groups called herds. A herd is made of moms, grandmas, aunts, and sisters, along with their young. The leader is most often the oldest female. She is called the matriarch. Over many years, she has learned where to find food and water, even when it is dry. Young males stay with the herd until they are teens. Then they leave to live alone or with small groups of other males.

A baby elephant is called a calf. It grows inside its mom for nearly two years. That is longer than any other land animal! A new calf weighs about 100 kilograms. It can stand within an hour. Every female in the herd helps look after it. When danger comes near, the adults form a circle around the calf.

An elephant's trunk is its nose and upper lip joined together. It has thousands of muscles, so it can do many jobs. It can smell, breathe, drink, grab food, and greet friends. Most elephants also have tusks, which are long teeth.

They spend most of the day eating grass, leaves, bark, and fruit. They also talk with deep calls. Some calls are too low for people to hear. But other elephants can feel them through their feet.

Sadly, some people hunt elephants for their tusks. Parks and laws now help protect them.

versions.title: Elephants: A Family Led by Grandmothers
versions.text:
Elephants are the largest animals on land. There are two main kinds. African elephants live in much of Africa. Asian elephants live in the forests and grasslands of southern Asia. Both kinds are smart, and both need their families to survive.

Elephants live in family groups called herds. A herd is made of related females, such as mothers, grandmothers, aunts, and sisters, and their young. The leader is most often the oldest female, called the matriarch. Over her long life, she has learned where to find food and water. In a drought, rivers and water holes dry up. Then she can lead her family to places she remembers from years before. Young males stay with the herd until they are about twelve to fifteen years old. Then they leave. They live alone or with small groups of other males.

A baby elephant is called a calf. It grows inside its mother for nearly two years. A newborn calf weighs about 100 kilograms and can stand within an hour. Every female in the herd helps raise it. When lions come near, the adults form a circle around the young.

An elephant's trunk is its nose and upper lip joined together. It has thousands of muscles. It can pull up a small tree or pick up a single nut. Elephants use their trunks to smell, breathe, drink, and greet each other. Their tusks are long teeth made of ivory.

An adult elephant may eat about 150 kilograms of plants each day. So it spends most of its time eating. Elephants also send low rumbles across the land. People cannot hear many of these sounds. But other elephants feel the vibrations through their feet.

Sadly, some people kill elephants for their ivory. Parks and laws now help protect them.

versions.title: Elephants: A Family Led by Grandmothers
versions.text:
Elephants are the largest animals living on land. There are two main kinds: African elephants, which roam across much of Africa, and Asian elephants, which inhabit the forests and grasslands of southern Asia. Both kinds are remarkably intelligent, and both depend heavily on their families in order to survive.

Elephants live in family groups called herds. A herd is made up of related females, including mothers, grandmothers, aunts, and sisters, together with their young. The leader is usually the oldest female, known as the matriarch. Over her long life, she has gathered valuable knowledge about where to find food, water, and safe places to rest. During a drought, when rivers and water holes dry up, she can guide her family to distant places that she remembers from many years earlier. Young males remain with the herd until they are about twelve to fifteen years old. Then they leave and either live alone or join small groups of other males.

A baby elephant is called a calf. It develops inside its mother for nearly two years, which is longer than any other land animal. A newborn calf weighs about 100 kilograms and can usually stand within an hour of its birth. Every female in the herd helps to raise it, and whenever lions approach, the adults form a protective circle around the young.

An elephant's trunk is its nose and upper lip joined together. Because it contains thousands of muscles, it is powerful enough to pull up a small tree but delicate enough to pick up a single nut. Elephants use their trunks to smell, breathe, drink, and greet one another. Their tusks are long teeth made of ivory.

Elephants also communicate with low rumbles that can travel for several kilometers. People cannot hear many of these sounds, but other elephants detect the vibrations through their sensitive feet.

versions.title: Elephants: The Wisdom of the Herd
versions.text:
Elephants are the largest animals living on land. There are two main kinds: African elephants, which roam across much of the African continent, and Asian elephants, which inhabit the forests and grasslands of southern Asia. Both are very intelligent, and both depend on close cooperation within their families for survival.

Elephants live in family groups called herds, which consist of related females, including mothers, grandmothers, aunts, and sisters, together with their offspring. The leader is usually the oldest female, known as the matriarch. Over several decades, she accumulates valuable knowledge about where to find food, water, and safe resting places. During a drought, when rivers and water holes evaporate, she can guide her family to distant locations that she remembers from many years earlier. Studies in Africa have shown that families led by older matriarchs respond more wisely to the roars of dangerous lions. They are also considerably more likely to survive severe dry seasons. Young males stay with the herd until they are about twelve to fifteen years old. Then they leave and either live alone or join loose groups of other males.

A baby elephant is called a calf. It develops inside its mother for nearly two years, longer than any other land animal. A newborn calf weighs about 100 kilograms and can usually stand within an hour of birth. Every female participates in raising it, and whenever predators approach, the adults form a protective circle around the vulnerable young.

An elephant's trunk is its nose and upper lip combined. Because it contains thousands of muscles, it is powerful enough to uproot a small tree yet delicate enough to pick up a single nut. Elephants use their trunks to smell, breathe, drink, and greet one another. Their tusks are long teeth made of ivory.

An adult may eat about 150 kilograms of plants daily, so it spends most of its waking hours feeding. Elephants also communicate through deep rumbles, many of which are infrasound, meaning they are too low for humans to hear. These sounds can travel for several kilometers, and other elephants detect the vibrations through their sensitive feet.

Unfortunately, poaching for ivory still threatens elephants, and many have lost their habitat as farms and towns expand. Today, national parks, rangers, and strict laws work together to protect these magnificent animals.

versions.title: Elephants: The Wisdom of the Herd
versions.text:
Elephants are the largest terrestrial animals on Earth, and scientists recognize two principal kinds: African elephants, which roam across much of the African continent, and Asian elephants, which inhabit the forests and grasslands of southern Asia. Both are exceptionally intelligent, and both depend on sophisticated cooperation within their extended families for their continued survival.

Elephants live in family groups called herds, which consist of related females, including mothers, grandmothers, aunts, and sisters, together with their dependent offspring. The leader is usually the oldest female, known as the matriarch, who accumulates invaluable knowledge over several decades regarding the location of food, water, and secure resting places. During a prolonged drought, when rivers and water holes evaporate, she can navigate her family toward distant locations that she remembers from many years earlier. Research conducted in Africa has demonstrated that families led by older matriarchs respond more appropriately to the roars of dangerous lions and are considerably more likely to survive severe dry seasons, which suggests that accumulated experience is among the herd's most precious resources. Young males remain with the herd until they are approximately twelve to fifteen years old, after which they depart and either live independently or associate temporarily with loose groups of other males.

A baby elephant is called a calf. It develops inside its mother for nearly two years, a longer pregnancy than that of any other land mammal, and weighs approximately 100 kilograms at birth, although it can usually stand within an hour. Every female participates in its upbringing, and whenever predators approach, the adults form a protective circle around the vulnerable young.

An elephant's trunk is its nose and upper lip combined, and because it contains thousands of individual muscles, it is powerful enough to uproot a small tree yet sufficiently delicate to retrieve a single nut. Elephants use their trunks to smell, breathe, drink, and greet one another, while their tusks are elongated teeth composed of ivory.

An adult may consume approximately 150 kilograms of vegetation daily, so it devotes the majority of its waking hours to feeding. Elephants also communicate through deep rumbles, many of which are infrasound, meaning their frequency is too low for human ears to detect. These vibrations can travel for several kilometers, and distant elephants perceive them through their remarkably sensitive feet.

Unfortunately, poaching for ivory continues to threaten elephants, and numerous populations have lost their habitat as agriculture and human settlements expand. Today, national parks, dedicated rangers, and strict international regulations operate together to protect these magnificent and ecologically important animals.

questions.stem: What is this article mostly about?
options: Why elephants are afraid of small mice
How elephant families live and stay safe
How to teach an elephant to carry people
Where to see elephants at the zoo
questions.why: Most of the article tells how elephants live in a herd, care for calves, use their trunks, and are kept safe.

wrong.A: The article never talks about mice.
wrong.C: The article does not explain how to train elephants.
wrong.D: Zoos are not part of the article.

questions.stem: Who leads an elephant herd?
options: A young male
The newest calf
The oldest female
The biggest male
questions.why: The article says the leader of the herd is the oldest female, the oldest mom.

wrong.A: Young males leave the herd when they grow up, so they do not lead it.
wrong.B: A calf is a baby. It needs the herd to keep it safe.
wrong.D: The herd is made of moms, aunts, and young ones, and its leader is a female.

questions.stem: Which things can an elephant do with its trunk?
options: See in the dark
Store water for weeks
Chew hard food
Smell, drink, and grab food
questions.why: The article says the trunk can smell, drink, and grab food, and it can hug, too.

wrong.A: Elephants see with their eyes, not their trunks.
wrong.B: The article does not say the trunk stores water for weeks.
wrong.C: Elephants chew with their teeth, not their trunks.

questions.stem: Why does the herd follow the oldest female?
options: She knows where to find food and water.
She is the smallest one in the herd.
She has no calves to look after.
She is the only one who can walk far.
questions.why: The article says the leader knows where to find food and water, so following her helps the whole family.

wrong.B: The article says she is the oldest, not the smallest.
wrong.C: The article does not say this, and all the moms care for the calves.
wrong.D: The whole herd walks together, so she is not the only one who can walk far.

questions.stem: The whole herd helps keep a calf safe. What does this tell you about elephants?
options: Calves can take care of themselves.
Elephants in a herd care for each other's young.
Only the mother cares about the calf.
Elephants do not like baby elephants.
questions.why: If all the moms and aunts help, then elephants care for young ones that are not only their own.

wrong.A: A calf needs help. That is why the herd keeps it safe.
wrong.C: The article says the whole herd helps, not just the mother.
wrong.D: The herd protects calves, so elephants clearly care about them.

questions.stem: Read the sentences: "Some have two long teeth. They are tusks." What are tusks?

Strong thick feet
Very long teeth
Short gray tails
questions.why: The sentence before the word tells us that tusks are two long teeth.

wrong.B: Feet are used to feel calls, but they are not tusks.
wrong.D: A tail is not a tooth.

questions.stem: Which sentence best states the central idea of the article?

questions.why: The article explains herd cooperation and the matriarch's knowledge, then ends with poaching and habitat loss.

wrong.B: The article presents elephants as intelligent family animals, not mainly as dangers.
wrong.C: The article says both kinds are intelligent and never compares them this way.
wrong.D: The trunk is one important feature, but the article stresses the family and the matriarch.

questions.stem: What did research in Africa show about families led by older matriarchs?
options: They traveled less and stayed close to rivers.
They gave birth to more calves than other families.
Their young males left the herd at a younger age.
They handled lions and droughts better.
questions.why: The article states that these families respond more wisely to lion roars and are more likely to survive severe dry seasons.

wrong.A: The article says nothing about traveling less.
wrong.B: The number of calves is not part of the research described.
wrong.C: Young males leave at about twelve to fifteen; the research did not discuss this.

questions.stem: According to the article, what is infrasound?
options: Sound too low for human ears to hear
A loud trumpet used to warn of danger
Sound that travels only through water
The noise of an elephant's footsteps
questions.why: The article explains that many elephant rumbles are infrasound, meaning they are too low for humans to hear.

wrong.B: A loud trumpet would be easy for people to hear.
wrong.C: The article says these sounds travel for kilometers across land and are sensed through the feet.
wrong.D: Infrasound refers to the low rumbles elephants make to communicate, not footsteps.

questions.stem: Based on the article, what would most likely happen if poachers killed a herd's matriarch?
options: The herd would quickly choose a young male as leader.
The herd might struggle to find water and avoid danger.
The calves would stop needing protection.
The herd would stop using rumbles to communicate.
questions.why: The article shows that the matriarch's decades of knowledge help her family find water and react to lions, so losing her would leave the herd less prepared.

wrong.A: Herds are led by females, and young males leave the group.
wrong.C: Calves stay vulnerable no matter who leads the herd.
wrong.D: Nothing in the article suggests communication depends on the matriarch.

questions.stem: Why does an elephant spend most of its waking hours feeding?
options: It must chew each leaf for a long time with its tusks.
It feeds only at night when it is cool.
It needs a huge amount of vegetation, about 150 kilograms a day.
Its trunk can lift only one nut at a time.
questions.why: Gathering and eating about 150 kilograms of plants takes a long time, which explains the long feeding hours.

wrong.A: Tusks are teeth used for other tasks; the article does not say elephants chew with them.
wrong.B: The article does not say elephants feed only at night.
wrong.D: The trunk can pick up a single nut, but it can also pull up a tree, so it is not limited to one nut.

questions.stem: "Many have lost their habitat as farms and towns expand." What does habitat mean here?
options: A herd's family members
The food an animal stores
A law that protects wildlife
The natural home where an animal lives
questions.why: As farms and towns grow, they take over the land where elephants naturally live, which is their habitat.

wrong.A: Family members are not lost because farms and towns expand.
wrong.B: Elephants do not store food, and the sentence is about land.
wrong.C: Laws protect elephants; they are not what farms and towns replace.

questions.stem: Why does the author include the research about older matriarchs?
options: To prove that lions are the greatest threat that elephants face in Africa
To show that young females should lead the herd
To support the idea that experience helps the herd survive
To explain how scientists record and study infrasound in the wild
questions.why: The research gives evidence that the matriarch's accumulated knowledge makes a real difference to her family's survival.

wrong.A: Lions are part of the study, but the point is about the matriarch's experience.
wrong.B: The research supports older leaders, not younger ones.
wrong.D: The research described is about leadership, not recording sounds.

questions.stem: Which two human causes threaten elephants, according to the article?
options: Poaching for ivory and the loss of habitat
Hunting by lions and long droughts
Zoos and noisy cities
Lack of food and cold weather
questions.why: The final paragraph names poaching for ivory and habitat loss as farms and settlements expand.

wrong.B: Lions and droughts are natural dangers, not human causes.
wrong.C: Zoos and noise are not mentioned as threats.
wrong.D: The article does not name cold weather, and elephants find plenty of plants to eat.

HIGH.prompt: The article suggests that the oldest member of a herd is one of its most valuable members. Do you agree? Support your answer with evidence from the article.
checklist: I supported it with at least two pieces of evidence from the article.
I explained how each piece of evidence supports my position.
